papers.title: Whose Side Are You On? Measuring Stance at Scale for Reddit Discourse Analysis During the Israel-Gaza War
papers.abstract: Large-scale discourse analysis often requires stance labels, yet for many high-salience political events such labels are unavailable at the comment level. We introduce and validate a comment-level stance measurement instrument that assigns Pro-Israel, Pro-Palestinian, or Undefined stance using Reddit comment text. The instrument is calibrated from a small, manually annotated gold-standard dataset and scaled through large language model-assisted labeling, achieving weighted-$F_{1}=0.88$ against held-out human annotations. To enable corpus-scale measurement, we operationalize the instrument as a lightweight classifier based on DistilBERT embeddings and an RBF SVM, which achieves weighted-$F_{1}=0.7935$ on the original gold-standard set. Applying this instrument, we measure the stance of approximately 2.7 million Reddit comments posted between 2023 and 2025 during the Israel-Gaza war. We demonstrate what this measurement enables by analyzing stance-conditioned asymmetries in sentiment, toxicity, and emotional framing across political affiliations. This work shows how validated, low-cost stance measurement can support large-scale descriptive analysis of polarized discourse, without relying on network structure or prior labeled corpora.

papers.title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel
papers.abstract: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

papers.title: What You Post Is What You Symptom: Estimating Psychometric Networks from Social Media Discourse
authors: Ana Sabina Uban (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
Liviu P. Dinu (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
papers.abstract: Symptom networks in psychopathology are estimated almost exclusively from self-report questionnaires, restricting inference to whatever symptom set a given instrument covers. We introduce a framework for symptom-resolved network estimation directly from social media discourse and apply the framework to depression and eating disorders, with a third anorexia corpus as cross-dataset validation. To our knowledge, we are the first to estimate symptom-resolved psychometric networks from social media text, compare them to clinical co-endorsement networks, and replicate transdiagnostic linguistic markers across 3 independently recruited corpora spanning 2 disorders simultaneously. For depression, expression scores correlate with BDI-II totals at $\rho{=}0.434$, 20 of 21 items reach FDR significance, and split-half reliability is 0.935. The Network Comparison Test detects few edge differences between modalities (3-5\% of edges), while bridge symptoms diverge. For eating disorders, the item-level results are exploratory. Identified linguistic features replicate the same direction across all 3 corpora, and they cluster in three construct families.

papers.title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
papers.abstract: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. I propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.

papers.title: Evaluating Cultural Reasoning and Robustness in LLMs for Spanish Political Discourse
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to interpret, generate, and mediate public-facing language, which makes their reliability especially consequential in politically sensitive settings. Although sentiment analysis is a common task in this area, affective meaning in social media discourse is often conveyed through culturally situated and pragmatically indirect cues that are not well captured by label-centric evaluation alone. In this paper, we evaluate the robustness of LLMs for sentiment analysis of Spanish political discourse from social media, with emphasis on culturally situated affective interpretation. We introduce a diagnostic protocol that combines three independent human annotation views into Gold and Ambiguous subsets, and extends the corpus with a Synthetic subset built from sentiment-flipped counterfactuals selected through model-conditioned perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge criteria. Using this framework, we compare proprietary and open-weight models under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, focusing on predictive robustness across human agreement conditions and counterfactual shift. Our results show that annotation ambiguity and counterfactual perturbation reveal failure modes that conventional evaluation on the original corpus tends to obscure. GPT-4.1-mini remains the most stable among the evaluated models, whereas the two smaller open-weight models degrade more markedly under synthetic perturbations, and few-shot prompting provides only limited gains. Overall, the paper contributes a reproducible protocol for robustness-oriented evaluation in political sentiment analysis, an empirical characterization of model behavior under ambiguity and sentiment-flipped counterfactuals, and a publicly available Spanish social media dataset with three-way human sentiment annotations.

papers.title: Minimum cores in lattice graphs: zonotope structure and quartic growth
papers.abstract: A core of a graph is a nonempty vertex set in which every member has at least as many neighbours inside the set as outside. We study the minimum size $c_{m,n}$ of a finite core in the graph on $\Z^m$ joining points at sup-norm distance at most $n$. The local majority condition imposes a global geometric constraint: the convex hull of every core has an explicit lattice zonotope $H_n^{(m)}$ as a Minkowski summand. In the plane, this zonotope has width asymptotic to $6\zeta(3)n^3/\pi^2$. We prove that all its lattice points form a core and construct a shell with $O(n^4)$ points. Together with a packing argument, this gives $c_{2,n}=\Theta(n^4)$ and coordinate widths $\Theta(n^3)$ for every minimum core. We determine $c_{2,1}=12$ and $c_{2,2}=96$ by analytic arguments and prove uniqueness up to translation in both cases. Explicit forced-set and deficit certificates determine further minima within the prescribed zonotope hull. We distinguish these restricted results from global optimality and state the remaining geometric conjectures. We also give a direct reduction from \textsc{Clique} showing that the core problem is NP-complete on general finite graphs, which settles a conjecture of Hassanpour in the terms in which it was posed.

papers.title: Effective and Efficient Rumor Assertion Over Large-Scale Social Networks (Technical Report)
papers.abstract: Nowadays, social networks, like Facebook, X, Reddit, YouTube, and so on, have become essential online platforms for users to connect with friends daily, post/share news, and express their opinions/comments. Meanwhile, however, the rapid and widespread dissemination of rumors and misinformation across social networks has become a serious concern. Such misleading information can distort public opinion and potentially cause significant social and economic consequences in real-world scenarios, including product promotion, elections and voting, and even cyberbullying. Therefore, accurately and efficiently verifying whether news spread on social networks is rumor or truth has become an increasingly important yet challenging problem. While previous works usually identified rumors by their contents, in this paper, we propose a novel \textit{user behavior model} to capture the users' judgment/discriminative abilities, which is learned via our well-designed evidence-aware probability reconstructor. We develop a general framework for tackling \textit{rumor assertion over large-scale social networks} (RA-SN), which can efficiently and effectively determine whether a given news item is a rumor with high confidence, based on users' behaviors, in a scalable manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed RA-SN approach on both real-world and synthetic graphs.

papers.title: Benchmarking Multi-Modal Graph-based Social Media Popularity Prediction
papers.abstract: Social media popularity prediction aims to forecast the future reach or influence of online content from early-stage observations. Accurate prediction enables key downstream applications, such as advertising optimization and strategic content planning by users, creators, and platforms. Despite substantial progress, existing popularity prediction works often fail to jointly consider multimodal content and temporal social interaction signals. Moreover, the literature remains highly fragmented across datasets, modalities, observation windows, prediction targets, and evaluation protocols. This fragmentation prevents fair comparison and obscures a systematic understanding of how textual, visual, temporal, and interaction-based signals jointly shape popularity dynamics. To address these challenges, we introduce MMG-Pop, a Multi-modal Graph-based Popularity Prediction benchmark, which unifies datasets, modalities, temporal interaction signals, and representative baselines under a standardized evaluation protocol. Furthermore, we propose MMG-PopNet, a unified multi-modal graph-based network that jointly models the aforementioned multi-modal signals and graph-structured social interactions. Extensive experiments on MMG-Pop across Bluesky and Reddit platforms demonstrate the superior performance of MMG-PopNet and yield new insights into cross-platform training generalization, multi-task prediction benefits, multi-modality contributions, and LLM prediction limitations. These findings establish a foundation for future research on social dynamics modeling and intervention under heterogeneous modalities and socially-aware agentic ecosystem paradigms.

papers.title: Beyond Satisfaction: Learning Associations Between Content, Reviews, and Well-Being
papers.abstract: Recommendation algorithms shape what people consume online, yet they are primarily optimized for star ratings, likes, and sentiment, signals of user satisfaction. Whether these signals capture what is good for users, beyond momentary preference, remains largely unexamined. Well-being offers an alternative target grounded in psychology that extends beyond satisfaction. We operationalize it as immediate and enduring expressions of the five PERMA facets in reviews. Empirically, immediate positive emotion and engagement cluster as more hedonic (pleasure-oriented), while relationships, meaning, accomplishment, and enduring positive emotion and engagement behave as more eudaimonic (meaning- and growth-oriented). Analyzing 13.7 million Goodreads reviews and the content of 16 thousand books, we study how PERMA expressions differ from satisfaction targets and which book content features are associated with them. First, satisfaction signals (star ratings and review sentiment) correlate moderately with immediate hedonic well-being (r = .43-.50) but less with its enduring expressions (r <= .28), and have almost no association with eudaimonic facets (r <= .09). Second, book content features are more strongly associated with PERMA facets (r up to .46) than with satisfaction signals (|r| <= .15). Content associated with immediate hedonic well-being differs from that associated with enduring and eudaimonic well-being: third-person pronouns and past-focused language relate positively to immediate engagement (d=1.14 and 1.05) but negatively to every enduring facet (d down to -1.58 and -1.32), while prosocial and achievement-oriented language relate to relationships and accomplishment (d=.45 and .96). These findings suggest that satisfaction signals capture only part of the well-being users express, and that well-being-informed targets could lead platforms to recommend substantially different content.

papers.title: Logarithmic dispersion at marginal stability in collective attention
papers.abstract: How cross-sectional heterogeneity evolves in nonequilibrium populations of competing, ageing units is a collective question that cannot be resolved from a representative trajectory or the ensemble mean alone. Analysis of more than two million age-aligned English Wikipedia page-view trajectories from six yearly cohorts spanning 2015-2020 shows that the variance of logarithmic attention grows linearly with $\ln t$, while the ensemble mean relaxes on the same logarithmic clock. This dispersion law recurs across all six cohorts and is systematically favoured over the tested power-law alternative; temporal increments also exhibit consistent antipersistent scaling. A complementary trajectory-level analysis reveals broad, non-Gaussian variation in effective relaxation rates, showing that this collective regularity coexists with heterogeneous observed trajectories. A minimal scale-free stochastic model combines mean relaxation with self-affine temporal fluctuations of age-dependent amplitude. Within this model class, logarithmic spreading emerges when fluctuation accumulation balances ageing attenuation, defining the marginal boundary between algebraic broadening and saturation. Together, age-resolved cross-sectional dispersion and temporal-increment scaling provide a transferable ensemble-level criterion for distinguishing amplification, marginal spreading, and saturation in other populations of competing, ageing units.

papers.title: Generalizable Social Bot Detection via Multi-Granularity Summarization and Domain-Invariant Learning
papers.abstract: Social bots are becoming increasingly sophisticated in mimicking human users, posing persistent threats to online information ecosystems. Despite substantial progress in social bot detection, existing methods often generalize poorly to unseen datasets. Two challenges underlie this limitation: heterogeneous user information across datasets makes consistent representation difficult, while distribution shifts encourage reliance on domain-specific patterns. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-Granularity Summarization and Domain-Invariant Learning (MGDIL), a unified framework for generalizable social bot detection. MGDIL first converts profile attributes into structured textual descriptions and summarizes historical posts into user-level behavioral representations, providing a shared semantic interface across heterogeneous datasets. It then combines task-oriented instruction tuning, domain-adversarial learning, and cross-domain contrastive learning to reduce dependence on domain-specific patterns while preserving discriminative information between bots and human users. We construct a unified instruction-tuning corpus from 15 social bot datasets, train MGDIL on 13 earlier datasets, and evaluate it on two later-collected unseen datasets under a temporally ordered cross-dataset protocol. Comparisons with representative conventional, neural, LLM-based, and transfer-based baselines, together with ablation and representation analyses, demonstrate the effectiveness of MGDIL in improving generalization across datasets. The code is available at: https://github.com/QQQQQQBY/MGDIL.

papers.title: Self-organizing recruitment cascades couple Levy search to a clustered maximum-entropy resource field
papers.abstract: Foraging recruitment is modeled as a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade on the group's communication network. Because activation is degree-normalized, crowding shuts the cascade off, causing the swarm to aggregate on a resource and then disperse to explore again. Acting on the cascade moves agents in space, rewiring the network; recruitment and exploration are thus one coupled process, and removing this coupling alone abolishes self-limitation. Recruitment spreads only within a connectivity window bounded below by percolation onset and above by degree-blocking. The swarm self-organizes to the near-critical edge of this window--self-organized quasi-criticality--hovering near but below the critical point without settling onto a size-invariant critical state, with a finite-correlation-time activity spectrum (Lorentzian-like, not 1/f) consistent with local criticality. Recruitment raises harvest up to 2.7x over solitary search on sparse, clustered fields and loses (down to 0.37x) on abundant or uniform ones; because resources generically aggregate, the favourable regime is the common one. The Levy search and resource field are both least-committal: a maximum-caliber walk coupled to a maximum-entropy point process whose generic sign is clustered, with the optimal search exponent tracking the field's fractal dimension. Heavy-tailed Levy exploration crosses sparse voids while recruitment cascades exploit clusters by switching agents to short local steps, binding exploration and recruitment into a single self-organizing cycle.

papers.title: Triadic and assortative structure of absorbing states in the Axelrod model
papers.abstract: We study the Axelrod model of cultural dissemination, viewed as a finite-state Markov chain on an arbitrary finite graph, and classify its absorbing states. An absorbing configuration splits the edges into interior edges, whose endpoints share their whole culture, and boundary edges, whose endpoints share nothing. A partition of the vertices into connected blocks is the domain partition of some absorbing configuration exactly when its quotient graph is properly $q$-colourable. The configurations with a given domain partition correspond to homomorphisms from the quotient into the $F$-fold categorical power of $K_q$, so their total number is a sum of chromatic polynomials over connected partitions; this gives closed forms for trees and cycles and the value $2^{n+F-1}$ for $q=2$ on connected graphs. In absorbing configurations no triangle carries exactly one boundary edge, the open-wedge mass of the interior graph is at most that of the host graph, and Newman's assortativity coefficients for domains, cultures and single features are ordered. The feature counts are martingales and their sums of squares submartingales, which yields an absorption-time bound of order $n^2$ that is attained on paths. Exhaustive enumeration and simulations illustrate the results.

papers.title: Network sampling: a comparative review
papers.abstract: Network sampling is essential for the study of real world systems, since access to the topological structure and dynamical characteristics of a complex system is usually infeasible, and can also prove computationally intractable for large and dense networks. However, the field still lacks systematic methodologies that allow a procedural analysis of sampling plans for connected data. Hence, this study aims to compare network sampling methods through the usage of multivariate statistical analysis and machine learning techniques that are anchored in network metrics' estimation of synthetic and real-world networks. It was demonstrated that no single sampling strategy dominates both cases, although Forest fire and Frontier sampling have presented the most consistent performance across all topologies investigated. The impact of each structural property of these networks for principal component analysis and classification results were also discussed, with consistent pattern groups seen for both data types. Transfer learning aimed at real-world network identification has also demonstrated that realistic structural connections can be correlated to well-known network models through the usage of sampled subgraphs' properties for model training, providing an avenue to real-world network characterization through sampling methodologies.

papers.title: LEDGER: LLM-Evidence-Driven Graph-Encoded Clustering-Friendly Representations for Short Texts
papers.abstract: Short-text clustering is important for analyzing user-generated content in social networks and online services, supporting applications such as topic discovery and user intent analysis. However, the desired grouping depends on an application-specific clustering criterion that general-purpose text embeddings may not capture. Large language models (LLMs) can apply such a criterion to a pair of texts without human annotation, and existing methods use their responses as generated descriptions, binary decisions or selected neighbours. These discrete outputs discard how strongly the LLM supports a pair and how many judgments stand behind it. Each judgment is also used alone or within the neighbourhood of a single text, so the relations that link judgments across the corpus remain unused. In this paper, we propose LEDGER, an LLM-guided graph representation learning framework for short-text clustering. LEDGER aggregates the repeated numerical scores of each text pair into an accumulated score and an observation count, which define an evidence target for every queried pair. The pairs whose scores reach a threshold form a relation graph, over which a graph encoder propagates text features with a propagation range learned jointly with the encoder. A pairwise predictor trained to match the evidence targets shapes the learned representation, and a distilled student encoder extends it to unqueried texts without further LLM requests. Extensive experiments on seven datasets with four frozen text embeddings show that LEDGER achieves the highest mean clustering accuracy and NMI against five comparison methods, and ablations show that the graph, the learned propagation range and the evidence target each improve performance.

papers.title: Disparity in Influence: A Fairness Evaluation of Centrality Measures in Complex Networks
papers.abstract: Social networks are shaped by homophily-driven connections, which naturally lead to the emergence of communities with uneven sizes and influence. Such structural imbalances impact the fairness of network analysis tools, particularly centrality measures that are widely used to identify influential nodes for tasks like information diffusion and network robustness. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive assessment of fairness in centrality measures, using influence spreading across networks with heterogeneous community structures. We first analytically show that disparity is bounded by outreach; cross-community outreach is bounded by the inter-community cut; and when all seeds lie in one community, disparity approaches the normalized outreach within that community as cross-community transmission vanishes. This explains why attenuation concentrates influence in the community where diffusion starts. We further evaluate a broad spectrum of centrality measures, including local, semi-local, global, and community-aware measures, on both synthetic network generative models and real-world datasets, using the Independent Cascade and Linear Threshold Models. The results consistently show that influence tends to concentrate within larger communities, with disparities becoming more pronounced under constrained or deterministic diffusion settings. We further observe that fairness is highly sensitive to the choice of centrality measure rather than its general category. In particular, fairness-aware adaptations of PageRank demonstrate a strong balance between maximizing influence reach and maintaining equitable distribution across communities. On real networks, these conclusions are largely stable under random removal or addition of up to 3% of the edges. Our findings highlight the need to explicitly account for fairness when designing and selecting centrality-based strategies in networked systems.

papers.title: "God says we are right!": The Interplay between Religion and Propaganda on Arabic Social Media
papers.abstract: Religion is a main aspect of life in many parts of the world; hence, it acts as a powerful tool for influencing people's views and actions. In the context of propaganda and misinformation, religion has been perceived as a factor that impacts people negatively leading them to be influenced by false or biased information. However, there are limited quantitative studies that explore the exact role of religion in this process. In this study, we investigate whether state-sponsored propaganda accounts share religious content in a different way than the typical norms reported in the literature and whether they mobilize this content to promote their agendas. This is achieved by exploring 15 Middle Eastern propaganda Twitter datasets encompassing around 124 million tweets from 32.5K accounts attributed to KSA, UAE, Egypt, Turkey, and Iran. We find that propagandists share excerpts from the Quran and Hadith according to patterns that reflect aspects of their state's agenda. We also demonstrate examples where such religious texts were used to modulate political messages.

papers.title: Changing a View Is Not Amending a Record: Timing and Visibility in a Model of Public Correction
papers.abstract: An accusation may remain on the public record after its author has changed their mind. Observers can respond either to what a person says now or to an earlier statement that has never been explicitly amended. We examine the consequences of these two signals with a generative agent-based model that separates private evidence updates, current expression, and revisions linked to a specific declaration. In paired worlds, evidence, prehistory, and opportunities to revisit that declaration remain fixed. When expression and amendment are synchronized and fully observed, the feedback channels produce identical trajectories. With sparse review, record-based feedback leaves 19.44 percentage points more eligible accusations unamended after 24 rounds (paired-world 95 percent bootstrap interval 13.89 to 25.31). The comparison averages 50 eligible worlds, containing 556 agents, from 128 newly generated worlds. Event traces show how a persistent public cue changes subsequent amendment propensity; an exact small-state calculation independently establishes the timing boundary. Reducing record salience can erase or reverse the increment, and a generic held-state process reproduces the dynamics. The findings show when current expression ceases to track correction of a particular public statement.

papers.title: All edges lead to Rome: analyzing Late Antiquity regime shifts using coin hoard data
papers.abstract: Complex network analysis and other statistical techniques can be fruitfully applied to historical data to understand dynamics that brought the territory under study to a certain state. In this paper we use the FLAME database to understand when a drastic change of trade regime occurred in the Italian peninsula by looking at mint-hoard links that are evidence of a physical connection between them. By using changepoint analysis to pinpoint precise dates in the time series of these links, and then historical as well as network data to establish the sequence of network collapse, we find that the demise of the Western Roman Empire started at the beginning of the 5th century AD, yielding a more precise sequence of how and when it reached Italia.

papers.title: Food co-purchasing networks encode geographic disparities in cardiometabolic health
papers.abstract: Unhealthy diets are a major driver of cardiometabolic disease, yet the geospatial structure of dietary behavior and its links to population health remain poorly understood. While large-scale retail transaction data offer a unique view of population dietary behavior, conventional approaches reduce purchases to isolated items, not accounting for how foods are actually combined. Here, we analyze 51 million grocery receipts across 95 Danish municipalities using a statistically validated bipartite network framework to isolate co-purchases that product popularity alone cannot explain. We find that, although municipalities buy largely the same products, their co-purchasing networks reorganize along a continuous urban-to-peripheral gradient in how those products are combined. The network backbone can be resolved into modular dietary communities whose local cohesion allows us to predict cardiometabolic prescriptions, explaining a quarter to a half of the variance left after sociodemographic adjustment, beyond what product prevalence alone accounts for. Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) show no spatial gradient in prevalence and are located at the network periphery, where they share baskets with fresh foods but rarely form the combinations that hold the network together. Taken together, our findings show that geographic dietary differences are encoded not only in what people purchase, but in how foods are systematically combined within shopping baskets, offering a scalable network approach for population nutritional epidemiology.

papers.title: Team Stability: Theory and Evidence
papers.abstract: Teams emerge organically when individuals decide on their own their activities and collaborators. I develop and test a theory in which teams form with consent, interactions reflect team composition, and payoffs feature externalities and several forms of congestion. Stability constraints concern group interactions and require each team member to be willing to remain rather than withdraw or pursue a project alone. Empirical analysis of research collaborations among economists at the Federal Reserve Board suggests that: (i.) these constraints help explain observed teams beyond the payoffs to collaboration; (ii.) estimated violations point to large teams of entrants that appear to be assigned; (iii.) a compensatory mechanism mitigates the effects of variation in policy workload, which appears to affect team composition more than total research output; and (iv.) shifting workload toward experienced economists increases entrants' research output and collaboration, at the cost of lower output among experienced economists who compensate for this shift in policy workload with increased interactions with entrants.

papers.title: Economic Power in International Trade
papers.abstract: Economic power is a country's capacity to harm another more than itself by withdrawing from a trading relationship. This paper develops a general equilibrium model of the world trade network to measure that power through counterfactual sanctions. Using a world input-output table of eighty economies and fifty industries, we solve for $3{,}160$ such sanction equilibria, one for each bilateral severance of a trading relationship. We read the asymmetry between the two sides' losses as power. Our results show that mutual trade dependence is anything but mutual. The distribution of power in world trade is highly skewed. In the median trade relationship, one country inflicts on its trading partner more than four times the loss it bears. Only one pair in seven is close to balanced. The United States is more powerful than all seventy-nine of its partners and China against all but one. Economic power is not determined by the bilateral trade balance.

papers.title: Regime-Uncertain Data Transactions: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Self-Adapting and Self-Diagnosing Multi-ML-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large firms use autonomous machine learning agents that communicate with each other across legal and geographic boundaries. The rules governing a particular transfer are fluid. They depend on where the data subject lives, where the agents operate, who their owners and targets are, and how many different versions of the rules are in effect. Descriptions of the data using tags can be inaccurate, and the counterpart agent may exaggerate its security measures.We model such a transaction between two ML agents as a regime-uncertain transfer game, with a third player acting as the enforcer. The set of rules is represented as hard constraints with a strictest-wins logic. Both agents maintain Bayesian beliefs about which rules apply. They can spend money to gain access to security measures and verify the counterpart's claims, and then negotiate within the remaining legal space using Legally-Constrained Nash Bargaining (LCNB).Using the Monotonic Concession Protocol with Zeuthen's rule, we design LCNB. We prove four properties of the model and implement it in a simulated setting with GDPR, DPDP, CCPA/CPRA, and a fictional stricter regime.Across three stress tests where residence and citizenship are at odds, the citizenship-based rule is violated in 21 to 37 percent of shared data records, while LCNB results in a violation rate of less than 1 percent.There are limitations to our results. With our default economics, LCNB shares virtually all aggregates, while having a low rate of violations partly due to this.

papers.title: Threats to the sustainability of Community Notes on X
papers.abstract: Community Notes are emerging as an important option for content moderation. The Community Notes system pioneered by Twitter, now known as X, uses a bridging algorithm to identify user-generated context with upvotes across political divides, supposedly spinning consensual gold from partisan straw. It is important to understand the nature of the community behind Community Notes, especially as the feature has now been imitated by several billion-user platforms. We look for signs of stability and disruption in the X Community Notes community and interrogate the motivations which may be driving users to contribute. We show substantial churn in the population of users who author Notes. We note that the majority of notes considered "helpful" (and therefore shown to users on X) is low, 10%, and declining. We conduct a novel analysis of the impact of having a note published, which requires being considered "helpful" by the bridging algorithm, utilising a regression discontinuity design. This allows stronger causal inference than conventional methods used with observational data. Our analysis shows than any positive effect on future note authoring of having a note published is unclear. This analysis has implications for the future of Community Notes on X and the extension of this approach to other platforms.

papers.title: Influence of Network Topology and Vaccination Strategies on HPV Dynamics: A Simulation Study Using the SeCoNet Growth Model
papers.abstract: This study examines how contact network topology influences the effectiveness of vaccination programs in the context of human papillomavirus (HPV) transmission. Using the SeCoNet sexual contact network growth model, we evaluate age based, ring based, and several centrality based vaccination strategies across the overall, male, and female cohorts, focusing on peak incidence, timing of peak prevalence, and cumulative incidence. The simulations show that degree, betweenness, and percolation centrality based strategies are generally the most effective, while ring vaccination achieves the greatest reduction in cumulative incidence among females. Network topology also plays a critical role: higher average degree reduces vaccination effectiveness, whereas higher power-law exponent, longer average shortest path length, and stronger clustering improve vaccination outcomes. The results highlight the importance of incorporating network structure into the design of HPV vaccination programs.

papers.title: Astro Generative Network: A Variational Framework for Controlled Node Insertion in Incomplete Complex Networks
papers.abstract: Empirical networked systems are often only partially observed: sampling frames, crawling policies, privacy constraints, and temporal gaps can leave actors and edges unobserved. This complicates robustness and sensitivity analysis because many graph-learning pipelines implicitly treat the observed node set as exhaustive. Link prediction and graph completion repair structure among known vertices, whereas full-graph generators synthesize new graphs rather than extending an observed one as a fixed backbone. We study the complementary task of controlled node insertion: generating plausible new actors and attaching them to an existing graph while preserving interpretable global topology. We introduce the Astro Generative Network (AGN), a variational graph autoencoder that samples latent vectors to decode node features and then integrates new vertices through similarity-based attachment to the observed backbone. We distinguish the recommended configuration, AGN, from AGN-original, a diagnostic baseline that permits generated-generated edges. Across three synthetic regimes, AGN-original forms dense generated-generated subgraphs that artificially inflate clustering and density. Disabling those edges removes this artifact while preserving degree and path-length behavior. In our experiments, AGN keeps clustering and modularity changes modest relative to pre-insertion values, while novelty diagnostics show non-trivial separation from existing nodes without claiming domain-grounded identities. Our contribution is methodological: a reproducible insertion protocol and evaluation lens for incomplete network science and engineering
